The camera's optical capabilities, as well as the image processing techniques, were thoroughly examined and validated through a range of test cases.

We examine $k$-Center variants in graphs of reduced doubling and highway dimension complexity. Our study focuses on the Capacitated $k$-Supplier with Outliers (CkSwO) issue and shows how it yields an efficient scheme with specific parameters when dealing with a supplier network of limited highway dimension and a limited number of suppliers. Conversely, we establish that a linear constraint is necessary to obtain an approximation for the limited doubling dimension case. This distinction highlights the differences in solving these issues and may influence how these problems are approached in specific network environments.

In our research, we establish the Bruck conjecture for the difference of entire functions and provide a precise approach to solving the Bruck problem. Furthermore, we derive a precise formula for the general solution of a first-order difference equation involving a small shift. Using this outcome, we obtain the solution to an associated problem where the difference operator affects the entire functions differently.

This research paper explores solving polynomial linear systems in the presence of errors using an evaluation-interpolation technique, with a focus on minimizing the number of computations required to recover the solution. This is crucial because it depends on the properties of the error matrix and the polynomial system, which can be unpredictable. Building on previous studies, we develop new, sharper bounds on the number of computations needed, taking into account variables and unknowns. Additionally, we investigate how these bounds apply in specific scenarios, such as when the error matrix has a limited number of non-zero entries or a particular structure. Furthermore, we propose an innovative approach called the "early termination" method to reduce the computations required, which is particularly effective in cases with restricted error patterns. These findings are validated by simulations and experiments that compare the improved solutions with existing alternatives.

In the ultrastrong coupling regime of cavity QED, we show that symmetry protects a type of photon bundle emission. The parity symmetry of the Rabi model allows for the creation of super-Rabi oscillations, resulting in the periodic production of even photons. The cavity phase error, inevitable in real systems, breaks this parity symmetry and makes the Rabi model dissipative. Despite dissipation, protected photon bundle emission still occurs through a many-body scanning process and is characterized by a scanning rate dependent on the Rabi period. Furthermore, we propose an experiment setup to observe this protected photon bundle emission.

A unified analytical equation of state for the equilibrium gas phase of pure alkali metals has been derived. This concise equation encompasses the perfect gas model, is applicable to all alkali metals, and has a broad range of pressure and temperature viability. Based on the equation of state, mathematical expressions for key thermodynamic properties and characteristics have been developed, including energy per particle, pressure, and specific volume. These expressions demonstrate the complexity of these properties decreasing with increasing temperature or decreasing pressure. This equation of state and associated properties offer a convenient and effective solution for tackling in-depth thermodynamic problems.

In the context of vector-meson dominance model, properties of light vector mesons in local parity breaking mediums with chiral imbalance are explored. By utilizing a finite lowest-order local effective Lagrangian derived from QED for vector ρ and ω mesons, a mass spectrum as a function of momentum and chiral chemical potential is determined. Furthermore, in addition to the existing Chern-Simons effect, which differentiates the transverse polarizations of these mesons, a significant radiatively induced contribution arises.

We have developed a reliable algorithm for estimating the scale of distributed networks consisting of nodes connected by edges, regardless of the number of faulty nodes that may intentionally disrupt communication. Our method works within a limited time frame and is capable of accommodating a large number of faulty nodes, as long as the network's connectivity remains strong. We tested this algorithm on small-world networks, examining how the estimated count compares to the actual network size and analyzing the factors that influence its accuracy. We have presented our algorithm alongside rigorous mathematical proofs of its soundness and efficiency. Additionally, we verified the performance of this algorithm through simulations under various scenarios of network disruption.

In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter patterns, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be solved to determine the metric variables in the initial data. Our novel approach modifies the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition by replacing the 2nd order Hamiltonian constraint with an algebraic equation, allowing for a choice of conformal factor instead of mean curvature. By bypassing mean curvature techniques, this method avoids introducing additional biases or artifacts. It's particularly adaptable to scenarios with intricate matter distributions and can be implemented with minimal adjustments to standard numerical relativity codes. Additionally, a suitable choice of conformal factor greatly reduces the 2nd order Hamiltonian constraint's nonlinear effects, making its solution significantly less complicated.

The main objective of the JUNO experiment involves a comprehensive investigation of neutrino oscillation by means of a large, centrally located, 20-kt liquid-scintillator detector receiving electron antineutrino signals from decayed radioactive isotopes nearby the reactor. To accurately measure the experiment's associated parameters, it is essential to understand the details of its detection system, including its photomultiplier tubes. To fulfill these requirements, an extensive testing program was conducted to thoroughly examine the performance of 20-inch PMTs. This program consisted of three distinct phases: a testing facility was built to examine the 20-inch PMTs' optical properties; a comprehensive study of 101 20-inch PMTs was carried out at the Borexino Counting Testing facility; and an examination of the remaining 20-inch PMTs was performed at the JUNO testing facility. This paper presents the results of the three testing phases, detailing the 20-inch PMTs' tested components, their examined properties, and the resulting data, including the 20-inch PMTs selected for the JUNO experiment.

In practical scenarios like power consumption forecasting and air quality analysis, long sequence time series forecasting (LSTSF) is indispensable. The complexity of multidimensional time series data presents significant model demands, necessitating precise representation of long-term input interactions and long-term causal influences. While traditional approaches like LSTMs and ARIMA have limitations, a new time series model based on an adaptive graph convolutional network (AGCN) has emerged. The AGCN framework effectively captures both long-term input interactions and long-term causal influences through adaptive graph convolutional layers and a long short-term memory layer. By incorporating a variable parameter selection method, the model can optimize parameters for better performance. The AGCN framework's superiority over baseline models has been demonstrated in experiments using real-world datasets, and its efficiency and generalizability have been validated through hyperparameter tuning and cross-validation.

Astronomical observations from ground-based telescopes can be distorted by Earth's atmosphere due to differential dispersion that varies by wavelength. Observations made off-axis, other than directly at the zenith, necessitate the use of Atmospheric Dispersion Correctors. Current designs of these correctors are based on atmospheric models which have yet to be verified through on-site measurements. We've developed a novel technique to collect and analyze on-site data on atmospheric dispersion, and have collected 261 data points across six distinct atmospheric conditions. Our on-site data not only affirms the existing formulae but also detects subtle discrepancies, particularly at wavelengths near the red edge. Moreover, our research suggests that the empirical model by Allen provides the most accurate predictions of atmospheric dispersion, and confirms the accuracy of the design of our Atmospheric Dispersion Corrector used in previous studies.

Recently, pre-trained models have significantly impacted ranking systems, delivering outstanding results. To balance high performance with computational efficiency, knowledge distillation is now extensively employed. In this research, we address two critical challenges in knowledge distillation for ranking models: 1) leveraging multiple teachers; and 2) utilizing label data within the distillation process. We introduce a novel distillation approach called PILE, which effectively addresses both concerns by iteratively calculating logits based on pair-wise sample rankings. By doing so, PILE can effortlessly incorporate multiple teachers and leverage label information, thereby enhancing student performance. Our experimental findings on real-world datasets, such as MSRA's Re-ranking and Microsoft's Bing's search, demonstrate the superior efficacy of PILE in knowledge distillation for ranking models.

Bosonic dark matter, modeled as an ultralight wave-like field near its Compton frequency, can be detectable even when its direct measurement is not sensitive enough to detect the signal directly due to its high frequency, because low-frequency fluctuations will occur as well due to its wave-like properties. A detector can therefore look for these low-frequency fluctuations, rather than its high frequency oscillations, as evidence of its being a bosonic dark matter candidate. Since these low-frequency fluctuations can occur simultaneously, they will exhibit cross-correlations, known as intensity correlations, which can serve as strong evidence for its being a bosonic dark matter candidate. In this research, we present a detection method based on this principle, by first deriving mathematical formulas describing how these low-frequency fluctuations behave, and simulating the performance of this detection method in various conditions. In our simulation results, we find that this detection method can perform better than current experimental setups and can reach a sensitivity that is several orders of magnitude better than existing benchmarks, while also being capable of distinguishing this signal from background noise effectively.

A key challenge in inverse problems like imaging and signal reconstruction involves finding a sparse solution to an underdetermined equation system, which can be achieved through various optimization techniques. In the context of 'basis pursuit', this sparsity is measured by a monotone, Lipschitz-continuous functional, and our study makes the assumption that a unique sparse solution exists and is strictly convex. By establishing the equivalence between this sparsity and the level sets of a specific regularization method, and utilizing the uniqueness of the solution to the associated monotone inclusion problem, we prove the existence and uniqueness of the solution to the basis pursuit. Our approach also enables the development of a computable algorithm based on the forward-backward algorithm.

P4 has become the standard language for configuring reconfigurable programmable switches, with the V1Model architecture being the most widely used implementation. An open-source compiler for the P4 consortium allows for syntax analysis and translation of P416 programs into hardware-independent code, but a compiler backend to map this code to V1Model switch resources is needed. A freely available compiler backend for P416 programs and V1Model architecture-based switches has been missing, hindering efficient programmable switch development. Our research fills this gap by developing an open-source compiler backend for the V1Model architecture, utilizing a new constraint-based solver to optimize P416 programs and reduce hardware requirements. A version of this compiler has been publicly released at https://github.com/p4switches/p416-compiler.

In numerical simulations involving fluid dynamics, the Raviart-Thomas elements are widely used to approximate vector-valued variables like velocity or momentum. Nevertheless, the standard finite element methods that employ the lowest-order quadrilateral Raviart-Thomas elements tend to have spatial errors and time errors that are generally not compatible when used in conjunction with the explicit Euler and Crank-Nicolson time integration schemes. To mitigate this issue, a novel time-integration approach called the "staggered time steps" method has been developed for vector-transport equations with a particular focus on the momentum-conservation equation. By incorporating the staggered technique, the spatial errors of the finite element method can be made compatible with the time step. To achieve this, the algorithm employs two consecutive time steps: the first involves solving a linear system to update a coarse-resolution approximation of the vector, and the second involves solving another linear system to update a fine-resolution copy of the vector by projecting the coarse-resolution result onto a higher-frequency space. To complement this approach, two distinct nonlinear filtering techniques have been formulated to ensure that the final vector approximation satisfies certain unitary conditions, thereby making it more accurate and consistent. To verify the efficacy of the proposed method, comprehensive numerical simulations have been conducted using complex geometries featuring a mix of both convex and concave surfaces. These tests demonstrate that the staggered technique combined with the explicit Euler scheme and a specially modified filtering algorithm achieves a precise vector approximation that is within a few percent error in complex geomet

The remarkable effectiveness of deep learning has sparked various concerns regarding ethics, particularly with regard to fairness and privacy. To address these challenges, researchers integrated fairness into deep learning models through regularization techniques and fairness metrics, ultimately achieving notable improvements. Notably, the emergence of federated learning has highlighted the need to simultaneously optimize machine learning accuracy, privacy, and fairness when dealing with diverse datasets. This study proposes a novel framework that seamlessly integrates differential privacy and fairness into federated learning, yielding accurate and ethically sound models. The framework's privacy differential analysis and fairness assessment are grounded in mathematical proofs, demonstrating how specific parameters influence both metrics. The experimentally determined trade-offs between accuracy, privacy, and fairness provide insights for parameter optimization.

Scientists analyzed collision data from the LHCb experiment to identify excited states of a particular subatomic particle, known as the B-c plus. They found two peaks in the data, each corresponding to a possible state. One state has a mass of around 6841.2 MeV and fits expectations for a particular predicted state. A second state has a mass of around 6872.1 MeV and may be consistent with a different predicted state.

In the last few years, the creation of accurate numerical solutions for problems with Hamiltonian dynamics led to the establishment of a specific class of energy-preserving Runge-Kutta methods known as Hamiltonian Boundary Value Methods (HBVMs). These methods can be interpreted as a continuous, multi-step approach, similar to Runge-Kutta methods but with continuous stages, and are explored here in the context of more general differential problems.

This paper introduces an innovative approach called local critic training, a model-parallel learning method utilizing specialized networks to refine neural network updates. The method's efficiency in reducing gradient communication cost is demonstrated with an analysis of variance (ANOVA) decomposition applied to the error surface. The results show that using multiple local critics instead of a single global critic significantly speeds up convergence and significantly lowers communication frequency. The proposed local critic training method achieves this improvement with only a minimal increase in computational cost and without sacrificing accuracy in large deep neural networks. The method's effectiveness is validated through experiments on convolutional neural networks and residual networks trained on the CIFAR-10 and ImageNet datasets.

Three-dimensional chaotic scattering has garnered less attention than its two-dimensional counterpart. In this research, a three-dimensional open Hamiltonian system is analyzed where the non-dissipative boundaries initially exhibit Wada behavior. Focusing on the effects of dissipation, this study finds that weak dissipation has both positive and negative consequences. On one hand, it causes the Wada basins to shrink. On the other hand, it increases the Wada basin's dimension. Moreover, this three-dimensional system's characteristics differ from a similar two-dimensional system, demonstrating the complexities of three-dimensional chaotic scattering.

A theoretical model involving an intricate scalar field that connects to three fundamental forces - the strong nuclear force, the electroweak force, and gravity - is being developed. This scalar field, denoted $\phi$, has unique properties that allow it to interact with Standard Model fermions while also possessing attributes necessary for communicating with gravity. The interaction between $\phi$ and fermions varies based on their flavor, which is a natural occurrence in this model. The study focuses on the most challenging type of interaction, which involves changes within the same quark or lepton group, but explores uncharted territory by including different quark flavors. To understand the flavor-changing process, a series of measurements from mesons are analyzed under various conditions. Additionally, a search for $\phi$ is conducted across various mass ranges using a specific type of meson decay. As a result of these analyses, desired characteristics of $\phi$ are established in relation to its mass, a specific ratio, and certain decay widths. These findings have implications for understanding the nature of $\phi$ and its attributes.

Human action understanding in complex videos has far-reaching implications, 
which this study addresses by proposing the Hierarchical Attention Network (HAN).
Compared to current deep learning-based methods, HAN stands out due to its
capacity for (1) extended temporal structure capture; (2) explicit modeling of 
temporal transitions between frames and segments, and (3) the ability to learn key 
regions in frames and temporal segments through its multi-step attention mechanism.
Evaluations of the model on established action recognition benchmarks indicate
remarkable performance superiority.

Investigating the thermodynamics and cosmic censorship conjecture in Reissner-Nordström anti-de Sitter black holes required us to calculate the thermodynamic variables of the thermofield double state formed from a scalar field in the near horizon region of these black holes. A near extremal black hole was subjected to a small amount of energy and then underwent extreme tests of the cosmic censorship conjecture by analyzing the properties of its resulting state. Similarly, an extremely non-extremal black hole was given a massive amount of energy and the properties of its resulting state were examined. Our findings confirm the validity of the cosmic censorship conjecture in this scenario and also demonstrate that the scalar field's dynamics can be described by a Schroedinger equation with a specific potential function.

This article will examine the concept of star formation (SF) through observation, and its progression over time, offering a fresh understanding of the process, particularly relevant since planet formation emerges from it and sheds new light on the origins of life in the universe.

This paper proposes a new computational method to estimate uncertainty and relevance metrics, like Shannon entropy and mutual information, for complex probability distributions that can't be directly calculated. By leveraging Nested Sampling, this approach enables evaluation of such quantities even when only sampling data is available. Three case studies are provided to illustrate its effectiveness: one with a straightforward Gaussian distribution; another with a real-world experiment involving observation scheduling for signal period estimation; and a scenario with predicting future outcomes from past data under heavy-tailed conditions.

We re-examine a widely accepted model for complex semiconductor production lines and analyze it in the context of states, controls, and input constraints within a fixed time framework. 

Extending existing research, we establish the existence of weak solutions that comply with measure constraints for this conservation law, and confirm that these solutions maintain a limited amount of variation within a specified time frame. 

We demonstrate that solutions with zero variation within a fixed time frame are optimal, and as the time approaches infinity, solutions exhibit bounded growth in variation. 

Additionally, we establish a crucial relationship known as a Large Time Discrepancy Principle, which enables us to derive optimal solutions by taking the limit of solutions optimized for smaller time frames.

Cybersecurity has gained significant importance over recent years, with the detection of cyber threats emerging as a critical task due to the immense damage a single breach can inflict on companies. The incorporation of artificial intelligence (AI) into this task has improved efficiency but identifying the ideal combination of features and learning algorithms remains an ongoing challenge. Conventional machine learning methods are hindered by complex datasets and the difficulty in extracting meaningful information from them. This research proposes a new attack classification framework called NBcoded, which combines network traffic data encapsulation with Naive Bayes classifiers to effectively detect cyber threats. The encapsulation process transforms data into compressed features, eliminating the need for extensive data collection and making the system lightweight and efficient. This compressed data is then fed into a Naive Bayes classifier, which utilizes probabilities to accurately identify malicious network traffic. This research also outlines a novel dataset, referred to as ZN1, comprised of 50,000 network traffic samples, which can be utilized for training and testing cyber threat detection systems. Experiments demonstrate that NBcoded outperforms existing classifiers, such as Multinomial Naive Bayes and Logistic Regression, in identifying malicious traffic with high accuracy, particularly when data is compressed into binary features.

For finitely generated groups G, the focus of this article is the geometric property of growth in graphs representing actions of G. Specifically, we investigate the growth of orbits produced by a finite-pass action, which has implications for G's linear representations. We also establish a criterion for an orbit-orocerde to attain its maximum growth rate sooner, and this result is relevant to classifications of finite-pass actions in certain groups. Lastly, this research leads to a classification of geometric finite-pass actions in a particular class of groups (the solvable groups).

Animals move through their environments for different purposes such as foraging, settling into a habitat, capturing prey, evading predators, mating, and protecting their territory. The intricate dance of species interactions is significantly influenced by the complex patterns of animal movement through their environments, which are often undetectable to the human eye. To uncover this hidden world, researchers have employed computer-assisted analysis of animal behavior captured through video footage. This paper reviews various methods used to locate animals in videos, which are essential for computing their movement patterns across their habitats. It also discusses algorithms for tracking animals over time, both individually and collectively, as well as in groups, and explores applications such as species identification and the quantification of animal interactions.

Maximizing efficient electricity usage across transmission power networks requires optimized surplus management to minimize costs.
In our study, we demonstrated the effectiveness of using quantum annealing for optimizing power networks by defining the QUBO problem and implementing solutions on both purely quantum and hybrid architectures.
The D-Wave hybrid solver and classical solvers on Azure Quantum were utilized to solve the problem, yielding hybrid approaches that outperformed classical methods in solution quality due to lower objective function values, regardless of problem size variations.

Artificial intelligence's capacity for independent, self-driven learning has been greatly enhanced by deep learning's advancements, yet its potential to bring about new, physically significant insights remains largely untapped. We argue that deep learning's predictive capabilities on large datasets can indeed lead to the discovery of universal physical laws and notable discrepancies. Our own research examples, involving energy usage and atmospheric conditions, demonstrate deep learning's ability to extract complex, physics-driven patterns from real-world data. We contend that the process of learning from data can efficiently pinpoint areas where deep neural networks diverge from physically grounded theories.

This study employs the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider to investigate the presence of hypothetical heavy, charged, long-lived particles in proton-proton collisions at a 13 TeV center-of-mass energy. The research draws on data collected during 2015-2018 with a total luminosity of 139 inverse femtobarns. The analysis focuses on a signature involving significant energy loss and excessive track formation in the detector, consistent with the long-lived particle decaying into a standard model particle and a light quark. The investigation explores the mass and lifetime of these particles, with mass constraints ranging from 400 GeV to 3 TeV and lifetimes ranging from 0.1 ps to 10 ns. The results are parameterized in terms of the decay length and velocity of the particle, with the study ultimately ruling out the production of the $Z_{\rm c}^{2}$ in its natural state and setting limits on the production of other long-lived particles 12 orders of magnitude stronger than current theoretical models at 3 TeV mass and 10 ns lifetime over three specific models.

We have developed a numerical approach to maximize coupling efficiency in single-photon sources consisting of a quantum dot and a ridge waveguide. Our design features a quantum dot positioned within an optical mode that exhibits low divergence and high optical power along the waveguide. The combination of the quantum dot and this optical mode enables efficient emission of single photons. The numerical simulation of our device reveals an enhanced single-photon emission efficiency of about 67% when compared to a conventional linear cavity. The improved efficiency is mainly due to an optical mode with low divergence that allows us to achieve high optical power along the waveguide. The numerical simulation of our device also shows the potential for high single-photon emission efficiency and high optical power along the waveguide even when there is surface roughness within the linear cavity. However, surface roughness within the linear cavity results in reduced single-photon emission efficiency and lower optical power along the waveguide when compared to a smooth surface. The numerical simulation of our device reveals that surface roughness within the linear cavity results in reduced single-photon emission efficiency and lower optical power along the waveguide.

Neutron inelastic scattering is a valuable tool that not only allows for the identification of a glass's vibrational modes near its boson peak, but also provides insight into the specific motions involved. Experiments have demonstrated that the boson peak is not just a singular frequency, but rather a complex aspect of a glass's vibrational spectrum that varies depending on the material and its density. The interpretation of neutron scattering data requires a comprehensive understanding of a glass's atomic structure, as local fluctuations and their corresponding movement play a significant role in determining the boson peak's characteristics. The recent advancement of theoretical models and simulations has enhanced our ability to predict and analyze the boson peak, thereby providing a more in-depth understanding of a glass's unique dynamics.

Particle physics is becoming a precise science driven by theoretical predictions, 
essential for analyzing experimental data. Future experiments like the LHC 
require advanced computations to understand single-particle behavior and 
production processes. These calculations involve extremely complex equations, 
beyond current analytical methods' capabilities. This study proposes a new 
approach, using differential equations with the majority of integrals evaluated 
numerically, and verifying its efficacy through a complex calculation. These 
results will be crucial for upcoming studies.

In random systems, the scattering matrix correlates incident wave patterns with internal distributions within a specified volume. A recently studied aspect is the presence of "eigenchannels" - specialized correlations that allow for optimized energy deposition. This research derives mathematical expressions for total deposited energy within these eigenchannels and validates two fundamental "sum rules" - the conservation of energy and the closed-system boundary conditions - in the context of scattering. A method for measuring deposited energy is proposed, along with the investigation of two experimental setups. Computations are conducted for a specific scenario with varied properties.

Researchers have identified a new spiral arm in the Milky Way galaxy: the Far 3-Kpc Arm. This arm's existence was hypothesized based on previous observations of the Galaxy Plane Survey and the Spitzer Galactic Plane Survey. To confirm its presence, they re-analyzed data from these studies and found consistent results. The Far 3-Kpc Arm likely originated around 13 million years ago due to a galactic collision that also formed another feature, a near arm. Both arms are thought to be mirrored by a corresponding northern structure. This new discovery changes our understanding of the Galaxy's mass distribution and the rate of its star formation.

Increasingly, optimization methods are being employed to uncover a broad range of solutions. Our comparison of multi-solution optimization approaches reveals that diverse solution sets often correlate with a higher number of valid solutions found. In multi-objective optimization, a key factor influencing the variety of Pareto-optimal solutions lies in the trade-off surface's shape. Conversely, in multi-task evolutionary algorithms, phenotypic diversity is facilitated by tasks' interactions and the algorithm's information-sharing mechanisms. Moreover, we find that utilizing similarity-based groupings to distribute tasks among separate optimization processes yields more extensive solution variability than task clustering, especially when disparate tasks are involved.

The Stable Roommates problem (SR) involves a set of men and women, where individual preferences are pairwise and asymmetric, while men's valuations are linear additively, leading to a novel class of preferences, thereby expanding upon existing theoretical frameworks. Under these preferences, we define stable matchings that adhere to certain constraints, such as ensuring women's preferences are fully respectful and men's valuations are respectfully incurred. In three-dimensional (3D) SR, we increase the dimensionality by providing each agent with three separate lists of preferences. This extension in dimensions complicates the existing 2D framework, particularly in regards to preserving men's valuations satisfaction. As a result, what may initially seem achievable - maintaining women's preference satisfaction - could potentially come at the cost of incuring men's valuations, highlighting a trade-off. In order to tackle this challenge, we establish a threshold, ε, where a stable matching can guarantee that the incurred valuations loss for each man is minimal, albeit slightly greater than ε. If ε is set to zero, the problem may become infeasible, indicating the presence of an ε-transition in SR's complexity framework.

Our research explores how new mechanisms of electron-phonon interaction affect valley behavior in two-dimensional materials. Typically, low-dimensional systems that exhibit valley degeneracy are inevitably coupled to phonons, leading to valley mixing and circularly polarized luminescence splitting. Theoretical models suggest that this interaction can be quantitatively assessed and that the resulting splitting is proportional to the phonon occupation rate, $\beta T$. We propose that this interaction can be utilized for the development of novel valley-based technologies through cryostable manipulation of carrier populations, and that these mechanisms can be efficiently mitigated using mechanical strain, allowing for the control of valley states without transferring heat to the system. Ultimately, understanding the complex interplay between electrons and phonons is crucial for the precise engineering of valley electronic properties.

We examine the class of all metric spaces with their distances measured by Gromov--Hausdorff distance. The subsets of spaces with bounded distances are called clouds, and their completeness is proven. The existence and unique characterization of the median space, which is the "average" of the spaces in the cloud, are also established. Furthermore, the structure of clouds consisting of spaces with a bounded diameter is studied, and the completeness of the family of their central spaces is proven.

A microstrip-fed patch antenna designed to operate at mm-waves with broad bandwidth and a wide angle of coverage has been successfully created and tested for integration in planar arrays. The designed antenna operates within a bandwidth of 11.1%, yielding a center frequency of 28.6 GHz, and exhibits an impressive signal strength of greater than 3 dB above the noise level within the 90 to 120 degree angular range. The achieved parameters result from the combination of a microstrip-fed patch antenna design and two strategically integrated metamaterial units that facilitate broad bandwidth and a wide angle of coverage, respectively. The optimized designed antenna produced signal enhancement of 5 and 3 dB when compared to a conventional fed patch and microstrip line, respectively, as well as a wide beam of 14.7 degrees at the broadest angle.

Large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing relies heavily on topological error correction codes like the surface code, underscoring the need for efficient and adaptable decoding methods, especially in the presence of faulty measurements. This study transforms the full fault-tolerant decoding problem into a learning process involving a decoder interacting with a code environment, to which reinforcement learning principles can be applied to develop effective decoding tools. Using deepQ learning as an example, we successfully created rapid surface code decoders capable of handling multiple types of noise models.

Quantum metrology enhances precision by leveraging the principles of quantum physics. This can be accomplished through interferometry, by first manipulating highly entangled quantum states and then extracting information about the target variable from their decay. The quantum jump approach offers a direct method for obtaining the maximum available information, making it particularly useful for complex systems by allowing for continuous measurement and simulation of quantum dynamics in the presence of noise. We have applied the quantum jump metrology method to a sophisticated system consisting of numerous interconnected cavities and derived an innovative algorithm capable of efficiently simulating its complex behavior.

The PHENIX Collaboration has collected data on direct photon-hadron correlations in 200 GeV/A Au$+$Au, $d$$+$Au, and proton-proton collisions. In Au$+$Au collisions, there's an asymmetrical distribution of hadrons linked to the direction of the photons, indicating that particles are traveling in the same way as the photons, and this effect is more pronounced at higher transverse momentum of the photons. This effect is found to occur across the entire specified range of photon transverse momentum. In $d$$+$Au collisions, a similar effect is observed on the near-side, but it's found to occur at higher photon transverse momentum and is limited to the Au$+$Au collisions below a certain range of photon transverse momentum. Both medium-imprint and initial-condition effects are considered to explain the observed phenomena. A potential explanation for the observed phenomena is that particles are traveling in the same way as the photons due to the transfer of momentum and energy from the medium to the fast-moving high-transverse-momentum photons.

In this hybrid digital-analog approach to quantum computing, any quantum algorithm can be implemented without traditional two-qubit gates by utilizing an inherent, always-active connection between qubits. Building on this principle, our research explores how digital-analog simulation can be used to study fermionic systems, specifically the Fermi-Hubbard model, using a fermionic SWAP network and a method to correct distortions. Focusing on the effects of qubit connectivity and the distribution of interaction coefficients, as well as the precision of entanglement-inducing operations, our results indicate that an optimal qubit connectivity arrangement for simulating fermionic systems of any dimensionality is a chain for systems without spin and a ladder for those with spin. This connectivity arrangement also facilitates the efficient simulation of systems with periodical conditions, essential for simulating bulk fermionic systems through periodic boundary conditions. An alternative method, the fermionic quantum circuit algorithm, is used as a digital-only approach for comparison. Moreover, our research shows that digital-analog simulations outperform traditional digital approaches in certain scenarios, specifically for systems with relatively strong on-site interactions and relatively few entangled sites. An analysis of the coherence time required for these simulations suggests that digital-analog simulations could be more feasible in near-term quantum computers, making them a potential option for studying fermionic systems where themalization times are involved, such as in the study of quantum critical behavior or the formation of fermionic condensates.

A common issue in machine learning lies in striking a balance between optimizing performance and robustly handling out-of-distribution (OoD) scenarios. Certain methods depend on intricate data representation, achieved through various forms of feature extraction or regularization. In this study, we establish a powerful new technique for creating rich features that addresses the performance vs resilience trade-off. Our method, an iterative process involving repeated optimization with specifically constrained data, produces features that yield impressive results with both Generalized Adversarial Networks (GANs) and Approximate Maximum Likelihood Collapse (AMLC). These features substantially enhance the performance of Gaussian-Wasserstein Barycenter methods and allow for the detection of OoD inputs with high accuracy. Furthermore, they demonstrate significant generalization capabilities in both settings, particularly when the testing dataset is created by modifying the training data, either by changing input image properties or text prompts.

Achieving the formation of intricate structures and rapid adjustment to new patterns in light-induced tissue modification techniques poses significant challenges. In this study, a novel system utilizing a field-programmable liquid crystal mask in conjunction with a standard spatial light modulator is proposed to overcome these limitations. The designed system incorporates an iterative training method to optimize its performance. By simultaneously projecting multiple patterns with distinct phases, the system enables simultaneous production of complex 3D structures with varying features. The results indicate that the system can effectively modify tissues with a resolution of 15.3 micrometers to create three-dimensional volumetric structures with features.

We appreciate the discussion opportunity facilitated by editors and reviewers. 
Sujay Sanghavi and collaborators correctly identified our approximation method's potential refinement by directly optimizing the lower bound of the ROITR's objective. 
However, our method's tractability advantage lies in its linear program representation, which often outweighs minor increases in computational efficiency for small sample sizes.
Regarding data release concerns, we agree that collecting specific patient data may be intrusive and that utilizing synthetic data with anonymization techniques could be a viable solution.
Regarding future research directions, we would indeed consider exploring the incorporation of additional constraints, such as the orthogonality condition, using semi-orthogonal polynomial kernel functions, and utilizing neural networks, all of which could potentially lead to improved T-Rule performance discoveries, especially the last option which could be a promising future area of inquiry despite its notoriously challenging non-convex nature.
Lastly, we would like to express our gratitude to the editors and reviewers for their thoughtful and insightful comments.

Monolithic CMOS sensors featuring small collection electrodes are an emerging technology, also known as small collection-electrode sensors or Medipix sensors. They have demonstrated potential in medical imaging applications at space agencies CERN's BEPC II and SLAC's KEK Belle II. The CLICTD device is an example of this technology, which was initially designed for space applications but has since shown interest in being used for particle physics applications as well. To determine the optimal substrate thickness for the CLICTE architecture, simulations were run and analysis was conducted on pad-designed CLICTD devices fabricated using different substrate thicknesses. The study also explored the impact of changing the substrate material, incorporating an ingot breaker, and injecting defects to analyze their effect on the device's performance. The findings from these experiments are presented and discussed in this paper.

Advanced technologies like advanced adaptive optics systems are crucial for gaining deeper insights into astronomical subjects, and fast atmospheric self-coherent camera (FASTAC) is an effective approach for eliminating turbulence-induced speckles in real-time. We've successfully implemented the FASTAC algorithm within an adaptive optics system and tested its effectiveness on various scenarios under laboratory conditions. Our experiments demonstrated the effectiveness of FASTAC in eliminating speckles across a range of speckle densities and wavelengths, and it did so rapidly, delivering over 400 outputs per second. This implementation outperformed a comparison method by 10 times, while also maintaining high performance even at higher levels of speckle density.

This study presents a novel exogenous model to tackle the challenge of negative interest rates, maintaining the mathematical ease of the Cox-Ingersoll-Ross model, and accurately replicating the observed yield curve. It combines the difference between two separate Cox-Ingersoll-Ross processes, incorporating the deterministic-shift adjustment. For quick alignment with the current swaption prices, the Gram-Charlier expansion is employed to calculate swaption prices within the proposed framework. Multiple numerical evaluations are performed, utilizing Monte-Carlo simulations to assess the impact of distinct parameters on the swaption prices, and to compare the Gram-Charlier prices to those generated by the Hull-White model.

Research into the characteristics of neutrino oscillations using active neutrinos may also lead to discoveries about sterile neutrinos, specifically in their associated parameters. We investigate the potential of DUNE, a forthcoming experiment, in searching for sterile neutrinos with masses in the GeV range. Our findings rely on the design of DUNE's Near Detector and the detection of neutrino beams from proton-ion collisions at 120 and 50 GeV in energy. We calculate the statistical significance of predicted sterile neutrino decays and observe that they could be detected at 5σ significance for 10-50 deg^2 neutrino-oscillation parameters and 10-100 GeV sterile neutrino masses. Additionally, we establish relationships between DUNE's sensitivity to sterile neutrinos and the capabilities of past and future experiments, particularly Borexino and the SHiP project.

Meta-analyses that include multiple trials based on shared study participants often report correlated effect sizes.  In such cases, employing cluster-robust variance estimators can effectively synthesize dependent effects, however these may produce inflated Type I errors in certain situations.  In order to improve the performance of the cluster-robust estimators when dealing with small numbers of studies, modified estimators have been developed.  Furthermore, when a priori knowledge exists as to which studies share participants, using weighted or model-based estimators can yield improved results.  In this study, we compare the performance of various meta-analytic estimators across four different scenarios: (a) effects sizes with unique variabilities, (b) effects sizes with identical variabilities but unknown, (c) effects sizes with different variabilities but a known ratio, and (c) effects sizes with different variabilities.  Through simulation of our first scenario, we find that the most robust estimators are the cluster-robust and hybrid linear combinations, however they may come at the cost of slightly biased estimates when the number of studies is small.  Moreover, when estimating variances, the performance of the modified, hybrid, weighted, and model-based estimators improves as the number of studies increases and outperforms the alternative estimators in terms of maintaining inflated Type I error rates when comparing true and nominal values.  Ultimately, based on our simulations, the hybrid meta-analytic estimator appears to be the preferred choice for

This study introduces an advanced integration method for simulating multiple colliding particles within complex flows. Due to the rapid time scales involved in particle collisions, traditional numerical algorithms often require excessively small time steps, limiting large-scale simulations. To overcome this limitation, we've developed a novel approach that separately calculates the movement of fluid and particles, using differently sized time steps as required. As a result, the simulation can more efficiently capture essential physical processes related to particle interactions, like accretion and collision dynamics. A corresponding correction method is also proposed to ensure accurate representation of turbulent fluid dynamics. Through comprehensive testing against experimental data, the simulated results from our approach match real-world observations with impressive accuracy, outperforming current simulation techniques.

Investigating the source of radiation energy in the Unruh/Hawking process has shed new light on particle number definition and as a result, the connection between energy-momentum tensors and particle four-momentum spectra. Two distinct methods were used to define particle number: geometric, associated with observer measurements, and physical, derived from energy-momentum tensors. These two methods were shown to be linked via a proof based on the Lorentz transformation property. Notably, the radiation energy originates from the gravitational field's energy-momentum tensor, which is explicitly demonstrated in the Hawking process case using a specific detector. This analysis clarifies the source of radiation energy and confirms that it arises from the gravitational field itself.

The effect of transverse momentum broadening on parton propagation through a large nucleus is investigated using various models in the color dipole framework. These models generate different values of a key coefficient that influence broadening calculations. Results obtained via numerical analysis are then compared with LHCb and ALICE experimental findings for nuclear broadening in the context of J/Psi particles.

This article presents $2$ distinct proof methodologies establishing the existence of pairs of relatively prime positive integers, $a$ and $b$, for which the following congruence is satisfied: the expression $a^2+ab+b^2$ can be factored as $7$ raised to a power of $n$.

The video explores the dynamics of a liquid jet that enters a channel filled with the same fluid. As the jet interacts with the surrounding stream, it becomes encircled by a sheath of entrained air. This sheath plays a significant role in the dynamic behavior of the jet and its penetration into the stream. Additionally, we examine the instability effects produced on the liquid jet and the consequences of these effects on its behavior in the context of fluid dynamics.

High-performance computing systems rely heavily on fault tolerance to prevent data loss and ensure system reliability. Recent advances in non-volatile memory have made it feasible to achieve this, as data in such memory is preserved even during crashes. Nevertheless, the volatility of system caches still poses a challenge, as data in these caches may be invalidated during a system crash. To address this issue, this paper introduces an innovative approach called algorithmic crash consistency, which ensures that data processing algorithms remain fault-tolerant by compensating for errors that may occur during execution. By integrating this approach into the Linux kernel, we can eliminate the need for costly checkpointing and restore processing efficiency in high-performance computing systems. Our experimental results demonstrate that the Linux kernel's current implementation already meets the criteria for algorithmic crash consistency, thus requiring minimal modifications to achieve crash-tolerant performance with improved efficiency.

Organizational frameworks like information hierarchies are commonly used to present complex data and simplify navigation, yet the automatic generation methods available today don't account for the interconnections in modern information networks. Presently, most techniques represent topics as abstract probabilities rather than tangible components of the underlying network, and many lack the scalability needed for web-based applications. In contrast, we propose a novel approach, Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), utilizing a non-parametric distributed processing model that effectively extracts meaningful hierarchies from large networks, even at a massive data scale, as evidenced by our experiments using three smaller datasets and Wikipedia's full content.

We conducted an exhaustive examination comparing two approaches: a statistical method for estimating escape probabilities in three-body systems and the standard numerical integration technique for analyzing binary star systems with a third particle. Our statistical method, grounded in flux-based concepts, was initially developed to resolve the long-standing issue of escape times in three-body systems and was found to accurately forecast escape velocities, orbital periods, and collision rates. Notably, our statistical framework predicted a critical density threshold beyond which escape is highly probable, in line with prior research. While the statistical approach provides rapid, precise estimates at the cost of a few hundred calculations, numerical integration offers more precise results at the cost of significantly more computations, primarily benefiting the binary star scenario.

Measurements of the nuclear modification factors of J/$\psi$ and $\psi$(2S) mesons were made in collisions of lead ions at the Large Hadron Collider in 2015. The study was based on data from both lead-lead and proton-proton collisions, involving a total of 5.02 TeV per nucleon pair. The findings show that suppression of both prompt and non-prompt mesons increases with the level of collision centrality, at an extent comparable to that found in previous 2.76 TeV collisions. The study also found that suppression of J/$\psi$ mesons over a specified momentum range varies linearly with the rapidity of the collision's participant region. The findings are consistent with a theory that predicts the suppression to be the same for both prompt and non-prompt mesons.

We propose an arrangement of predicates in continuous logic such that the
logical framework's meaning can be structured within a hyperdoctrine framework.
This hyperdoctrine can be incorporated into a hyperdoctrine representing subobjects on a suitable category of topological structures. 
To achieve this incorporation, it is necessary to adapt the hyperdoctrine framework for continuous logic and establish an equivalence between its underlying logic and that of a specific topological structure.

When designing a software system, a modification in one component may
unintentionally impact other parts, hindering overall system performance. This is
addressed by conducting regression testing, which re-evaluates system sections
aimed at preventing adverse effects. However, pinpointing these affected areas
proves challenging, making it essential to identify system changes through a
different approach. We apply singular value decomposition to group software
modifications by their functional roles, allowing for more efficient detection
of areas requiring retesting during parallel testing.

A new technique is proposed to forecast suicidal ideation based on the integration of Electronic Health Records and Ecological Momentary Assessment data utilizing advanced deep sequential models. These datasets comprise time series data, often plagued by irregular sampling periods and noise levels. Research indicates that the use of recurrent neural networks can effectively forecast suicidal ideation from Ecological Momentary Assessment data, though such models are susceptible to biases in sampling. To address this, the authors have successfully applied the Foresight Model, a state-space model-based approach, to forecast suicidal ideation from both Electronic Health Records and Ecological Momentary Assessment data. When combining the two datasets, particular care must be taken to account for differences in observation periods and noise levels. Towards this end, the authors have developed a novel method to forecast suicidal ideation from both health records and momentary assessment data, utilizing the Foresight Model, and proposing an algorithm to "align" the two datasets for joint analysis. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of the combined approach over methods utilizing individual datasets in isolation.

Our research reports a significant finding at a 4.9 $\sigma$ confidence level of linear X-ray polarization within a 3% error margin at an energy of 4.5-5.5 keV in Cassiopeia A. Multiple observations of this supernova remnant reveal varying polarization levels within a similar range for multiple angles. However, a common characteristic is the presence of circular polarization, detected at a 3.1 $\sigma$ confidence level. To better understand the complex interior of Cassiopeia A, we've applied both a straightforward and a complex model to interpret our results. In the first model, the polarization arises from the orientation of electrons, while in the second, it is influenced by both electron orientation and magnetic orientation. Our analysis also includes a test to determine if the polarization angles of both radiations are identical, revealing no connection between them. Our findings are consistent with the theory of electrons in a synchrotron radiation model, but further investigation is needed to determine if the polarization could also be influenced by magnetic fields. Our study on Cassiopeia A provides valuable insights into the extreme astrophysical environments that supernovae and neutron star collisions create.

Consider a set $\{a_1, \ldots, a_n\}$ of distinct positive integers where $a_1 < \ldots < a_n$, with the requirement that only subset sums up to a size of at most $\lambda n$ be unique. Erdos originally proposed a conjecture suggesting that $a_n > c \cdot 2^n$, with the current record at $a_n > c \cdot 2^n/\sqrt{n}$. This article presents modified constraints where we investigate lower and upper bounds for the minimum possible value of $a_n$.

The characteristics of dense matter within the density range of 1-10 times nuclear saturation density, present in compact stars, are intriguingly ambiguous and may influence neutron star dynamics as detected via gravitational waves.  As a compact star's mass increases, its density also rises, prompting a search for dense matter properties.  At higher densities, novel particles like kaons, yoghons, and others may form, altering the matter composition and equation of state.  We investigate the sound velocity in dense matter, considering various particles that could be present, such as kaons, yoghons, and others, using different models.  In this process, we also determine the gravitational constant for compact stars in dense matter with the presence of kaons, yoghons, and other particles, leveraging their spin-oscillation properties.  Our analysis on the sound velocity and these properties in dense matter may shed light on the role of potential particles and help develop compact star theories.

We investigate a combination of squeezing and displacement operations transforming the Fock space, mapping it onto itself, and reveal a key structural link within this space. Specifically, we identify a sequence of operations linking any two basis states in the Fock space, demonstrating that a certain type of nonlinear integer-valued transformation connects them. Furthermore, our research highlights a class of highly squeezed states that can be accessed and controlled, and shows that certain thermal states become perfectly pure when an underlying squeezing interaction is fully utilized.

During gas-liquid interfaces that are subject to irregular movement such as splashing and atomization, the resulting fluid structures can be intricate and embedded in their surroundings. In this work, we employ a technique called skeletonization to extract the fundamental information needed to represent their geometry. By applying a modified version of a previous approach that efficiently handles three-dimensional data, we obtain the skeletons of the interfaces and use them to derive essential characteristics such as branch counts, branch lengths, and branch splits. A method for evaluating the similarity of interfaces, useful for identifying instances where two interfaces are the same despite minor variations, has also been developed. We test the efficacy of our approaches by simulating and analyzing a millimetric liquid splash, demonstrating the feasibility of our methods for analyzing complex interface topology.

Researchers discovered that certain influenza viruses exhibit active movement on surfaces with carbohydrate layers and display dynamic behavior similar to that seen in active liquid membranes. They found that this movement is induced by the self-rolling of viral envelopes. A new study provides insight into this self-rolling process from both experimental and theoretical perspectives. Experiments revealed that the viral envelopes undergo complex movement on surfaces over extended periods. Computational models simulated the viral capsid's geometry and found that dynamic carbohydrate networks play a crucial role in the self-rolling process. The research has significant implications for the understanding of viral infection and the development of novel viral delivery systems.

We've examined over 9,000 massive, star-forming galaxies in the SDSS DR12 dataset, focusing on two types: those with tightly packed disks and those with extensively warped limbs. Our analysis revealed that galaxies with highly curved edges, referred to as U type warps, are predominantly found in groups and clusters and are more prevalent in larger galactic systems. Approximately 3% of these galaxies exhibit signs of ongoing tidal interaction. By comparing U type warps to a randomly selected sample, we've found a notable 23% of these galaxies display similarities to 'jellyfish' galaxies, characterized by their exposed disks and compressed cores. Upon further investigation, we've discovered that these U type warps are more likely to have dim central masses, higher spiral arm compression, and greater disk heights, all indicators of group/cluster interactions that lead to jellyfish-like phenomena. Our findings suggest two possible mechanisms: group/cluster galaxies with higher orbital energy tend to run into smaller galaxies, stripping away material and compressing their disks; similarly, galaxies with highly curved edges are more likely to experience compression, stripping, or other group/cluster forces that result in the jellyfish galaxy appearance.

This research focuses on harmonic functions within the context of a particular type of manifold where the Ricci curvature decreases over time and the scalar curvature remains constant. We have derived a key theorem demonstrating that bounded harmonic functions are constant in this specific type of manifold, without relying on an established growth estimate. Consequently, this result implies that the set of all harmonic functions that grow at a polynomial rate on these manifolds is finite-dimensional.

Compounds composed of potassium ($A=$ K, Rb, Cs) combined with boron in a 2:1 ratio, exhibit unique cubic structures called the Laves phase with a specific Fd$\bar{3}$m symmetry. The arrangement of atoms within these crystals permits the existence of chirally behaving phonons, which correspond to rotations in certain crystal planes. The total heat generated by these phonons is calculated using Debye's model for KBi$_{2}$, RbBi$_{2}$, and CsBi$_{2}$. The calculated results indicate that KBi$_{2}$ and RbBi$_{2}$ can be effectively cooled via laser light to temperatures below their respective Debye temperatures. The predicted cooling effect for CsBi$_{2}$ is less pronounced, possibly due to its lower Debye temperature.

In insulators, Born effective charges relate to the response of the crystal lattice to a local electric field, and their nonadiabatic counterparts are similarly defined for conductors. We have derived closed-form expressions for nonadiabatic Born effective charges in three-dimensional metals under three specific conditions: when local electric fields affect one band, when symmetry allows for simplification, and when there is no band approximation involved. These charges are contingent on the detailed configuration of atomic orbits within the unit cell. We have further demonstrated that the static limit of our nonadiabatic Born effective charge calculations is equivalent to a previously published formula. Notably, our findings show that the static limit of the nonadiabatic Born effective charge is directly proportional to the Drude weight, a measure of how well electrons can resist electric fields in metals.

We are modeling a fluid without borders and finding that thermal vibrations generate the decrease in energy in a highly chaotic fluid. Highly organized, or laminar, flow occurs below a certain speed threshold in these types of fluids; however, above this speed threshold, the fluid becomes highly chaotic and uniform flows are no longer possible. We are working with an extremely simplified scenario in which the properties of the fluid are the same everywhere and there is no viscosity. Even without viscosity, we find that the energy in these types of fluids decreases due to the movement and heat generated by thermal vibrations. We are using a highly advanced technique to solve these complex equations and our results are consistent with measurements from similar situations. We are also finding that the rate at which the energy in these types of fluids decreases varies significantly depending on the speed of the movement and the characteristics of the fluid. We are taking into account the movement and heat generated by thermal vibrations, and our results are also influenced by the rate at which the movements in these types of fluids change over time.

Three-dimensional topological insulators can be identified by a magnetoelectric coefficient with a quantized value, but it lacks observable manifestations when time-reversal symmetry prevails due to opposing influences from wave function and magnetic fields. A distinctive manifestation of magnetoelectric coefficient emerges when time-reversal symmetry is compromised, an effect that can be likened to a merged version of the nonlinear Hall effect and the Witten effect. A notable instance of this phenomenon arises in a topological insulator with a band gap, characterized by the quantization of magnetic flux due to edge states.

In systems featuring delayed nonlinearity, we observe chaotic diffusion as a typical trait, where it is found that modulating the time delay periodically leads to a significant enhancement of the diffusion coefficient by several orders of magnitude, often reaching its greatest value at specific points within the system. This phenomenon is independent of the system's initial conditions and can occur even when the modulated delay traces a highly irregular path. Our research involves analyzing a simple physical model based on a piecewise-linear equation representing an oscillator interacting with another oscillator affected by delay and subject to external modulation. By applying the Lorenz model's understanding and discovering analogous behavior in another model involving a combination of geometric and algebraic elements, we provide a simplified explanation for the observed diffusion enhancement. It is hypothesized that these findings may extend to a broader class of delay-based systems exhibiting chaotic behavior.

We provide rigorous definitions for sound and sufficient denotational and operational interpretations of the stochastic lambda calculus. By adapting established techniques to reason about high-level probabilistic code, this study achieves a breakthrough in linking operational and denotational views with a proven adequacy theorem, thereby closing a key outstanding issue identified in earlier work (Bacci et al., 2018).

Discussions among developers encompass a variety of interactions, including in-person conversations and online comments, which are beneficial to label as relevant to software design for documentation and improvement purposes. This is achievable through a process known as design mining, which applies machine learning to categorize discussions as pertaining to design. The primary challenge in design mining is enhancing the model's accuracy on unseen data. This study proposes a novel technique, conclusion stability, to enhance model performance by leveraging the strengths of multiple classifiers trained on different datasets. The technique achieves a satisfactory outcome when applied to a dataset consisting of discussion threads.

A proposed model explains the existence of gravity, dark energy, and dark matter.
Gravity results from a topological deformation of space-time caused by
post-inflationary energy releases. Dark energy and dark matter stem from the
maladaptive behavior of space-time's causal domains and residual zero-point fields,
respectively. Gravity, dark energy, and dark matter are inherent components of the
universe's primary holographic field. Data and observations supporting General
Relativity are consistent with this framework.

Proximal methods can efficiently uncover the underlying pattern in stochastic optimization tasks, and our study reveals that these methods successfully identify the stationary points of the objective function, effectively extracting useful information about the function's geometry. Building on this insight, we propose a new technique that leverages the results from the proximal methods' iterations to expedite convergence. Specifically, we show that incorporating the direction from the proximal gradient method at each step into the Newton method's update rule enables it to converge at a quadratically faster rate.

We are introducing a new concept called weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideals within a commutative ring with identity, which serves as an extension to the existing notion of weakly prime ideals. A prime ideal $I$ in a ring $R$ is said to be weakly $1$-absorbing if for every three non-unit elements $a,b,$ and $c$ in $R$ where their product is non-zero and within $I$, it follows that either the product of $a$ and $b$ is in $I$, or $c$ is in $I$. Our research shows that not all prime ideals in a ring are weakly $1$-absorbing, yet we establish the criterion for an ideal to possess this characteristic. Additionally, we have found the relationship between weakly $1$-absorbing and weakly prime ideals in a ring, along with a computation of the number of weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideals within a specific finite ring.

We present new findings for two semileptonic decay processes, $B^0$ decaying into $\rho^-$ and a lepton-neutrino pair, and $B^+$ decaying into $\rho^0$ with the same pair, utilizing data from Belle II's sample equivalent to 189.9/fb, collected between 2019 and 2021. The reconstruction of the neutral $B$ meson in the sample involves having hadronic decays into $\pi^+ \pi^- \eta$, analyzing the momentum and direction of the lepton and the hadronic system can help differentiate between true and fake signals, ultimately resulting in calculated branching fractions of $(4.12 \pm 0.47 \pm 0.19 \pm 0.30) \times 10^{-4}$ for $B^0$ into $\rho^- \ell^- \nu_\ell$ and $(1.71 \pm 0.40 \pm 0.21 \pm 0.22) \times 10^{-4}$ for $B^+$ into $\rho^0 \ell^+ \nu_\ell$.

Our team employed photonic technology to revolutionize the conventional method of spectroscopy, enabling on-device spectral cross-correlation using a template spectrum. This was achieved by designing photonic devices with intricately modulated transmission spectra, thereby performing cross-correlation without the need for dispersion. Consequently, our device simplifies the setup, diminishes error propagation, and reduces costs, thereby making spectroscopic analysis more accessible across a range of applications.

In the last few years, various machine learning models have emerged with the aim of tackling complex drug-related problems, including predicting compatible drug pairs, identifying contraindicated medications, and grading medication safety. A key challenge in achieving these goals is navigating the vast space of possible drug combinations. Despite the numerous proposals, a comprehensive overview of pair-scoring models is currently lacking. This paper aims to fill this gap by offering an in-depth examination of existing approaches, critiquing both their strengths and weaknesses, and suggesting promising directions for future research in the field.

This research contributes a novel approach for detecting road damage, which can operate in various environments. The method derives inspiration from the human eye-brain information processing cycle and is grounded in psychological principles. It effectively extracts essential information from images but lacks the human ability to replicate exact eye movements. Therefore, we utilize a transfer learning strategy with pre-trained models to facilitate efficient training. The proposed method's effectiveness has been substantiated through testing on multiple road damage datasets from the UK, Germany, and Australia. The results indicate that a well-designed approach with minimal modifications can successfully adapt to different environments and successfully identify road damage.

Imitation learning seeks to bypass the complexity of teaching a robot a task. By utilizing a human demonstrator, we focus on leveraging observations beyond the training system's environment to enhance imitation. Our model, ODIL, utilizes optical flow and system pixel data to establish correspondences between the demonstration and training environments. The main challenge lies in handling instances where the demonstration or training environment is unmapped or experiencing a drift. To address this, ODIL employs a dual-network design that predicts the other's mapping and tracks the demonstration's state and pose to optimize performance. Our approach demonstrates effective results on a mobile robot and is notably efficient, with a runtime of merely 30 milliseconds for inference.

A massive, rotating Population III star forms an accretion disk that has the potential to fragment and influence surrounding star formation. We model this star and disk system, incorporating the amplification of magnetic fields resulting from rotation and the effects of magnetic braking on the disk's fragmentation. Our findings, obtained by conducting superparameterized simulations, match those of an earlier study using MHD methods. We discover that the magnetic field's amplification to tens of milligauss has a substantial impact on the disk's structure and its potential for fragmentation. When the magnetorotational instability acts in the disk's outer regions, it produces complex, gravitationally bound structures, but these are always accompanied by a significant overdensity in the center. In contrast, structures formed in the disk's inner areas are largely unaffected by magnetic effects and are characterized by a notable mass overdensity. Our study indicates that magnetic braking has a significant impact on the disk's mass distribution and eliminates all signs of fragmentation by the end of the accretion phase. As a result, all mass ends up on the protostar, meaning that the disk's mass return to the star is likely to be substantial.

Association rule analysis is a widely used technique in Data Mining. This method involves partial implications between binary variables, which can be constrained by parameters such as confidence and support levels. In this research, we investigate minimum-size bases for association rules from a logical perspective, drawing on concepts like consistency and deduction schemes. A minimal base for an association rule (A=>B) comprises formulas that, when combined, logically imply B given A. However, existing approaches often fail to remove non-essential assumptions. By leveraging the notion of redundancy in logical formulas, we develop two novel algorithms to generate more efficient minimal bases. The first algorithm produces a base with reduced size by eliminating redundant premises. The second algorithm generates a base with the fewest premises, removing redundant ones along the way. We also introduce a straightforward method for identifying redundant hypotheses within existing base sets. Experimental outcomes confirm the superiority of our proposed algorithms to existing ones in terms of size and computation time.

Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently struggle with mental health disorders.  An analysis of North Carolina court cases between 1994 and 2009 examined how court-ordered mental health treatment as part of probation affects an offender's chances of returning to court, and whether this result is linked to reduced mental health issues.  The study discovered that offenders who underwent mental health treatment as part of their probation had a lower likelihood of being readmitted to court and evidence suggests this effect is also associated with improved mental health outcomes.  The research found that receiving mental health services led to a 14% decrease in re-arrest and re-admission to court, and among those identified with mental health disorders, this reduction more substantially at 24%.  Additionally, receiving mental health services was linked to a 30-day decrease in the time until the next offense and a 20% decrease in future convictions.  The study found that offenders who received mental health services as part of their probation had mental health outcomes similar to those who received traditional probation, and among those identified with mental health disorders, receiving mental health services as part of probation and as part of jail time resulted in improved mental health outcomes.  The study found small differences in re-arrest and re-admission to court between these groups.  In particular, receiving mental health services as part of probation led to a 10% decrease in re-arrest and re-admission to court, and receiving mental health services as part of jail time led to

The authors of the paper delve into generalized Apostol-Bernoulli polynomials with parameters, derive their generating functions, examine key properties and relationships, and establish connections to other notable polynomials.

Radio maps are being explored as a promising approach to equip advanced wireless networks with situational awareness. They will likely serve a pivotal function in enabling UAV communications by allowing the assessment of signal strength and interference levels at unknown locations. Different from conventional radio map estimation techniques, which depend on uncontrolled sensor measurements, a new method proposes that a UAV collect data at designated locations along a carefully planned route to quickly obtain a reliable map. This route is optimized using a measure that identifies the most informative locations to collect data from. A novel Bayesian algorithm is developed to create the map, using the collected data and the planned route. It's shown that these Bayesian estimates are accurate and reliable, yet computing them requires significant processing power. A simplified version of the estimator, using fewer parameters and requiring less computational resources, is also presented and compared to the original Bayesian estimator.

This paper outlines a novel approach, GLA, for identifying unusual patterns in discrete time series by leveraging Hidden Markov Models and adapting likelihood ratio techniques from traditional anomaly detection methods.
